query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The key to the unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr lies in an interplay between temperature‐dependent intrinsic thermal expansion mismatch and a residual dislocation network generated by cold working. In other words, as the alloy is cooled from its processing/annealing temperature, differential thermal expansion induces local internal stresses that modify and stabilize residual dislocation structures; these in turn control both the work‐hardening response at lower temperatures and the high‐temperature creep (by impeding dislocation mobility) while also affecting measured elastic moduli.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy produced by cold rolling (with notable residual dislocation bands) and partially annealed to retain some of the cold‐work induced microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled thermal cycling and stress‐relief annealing to remove (or minimize) the residual dislocation content. Compare samples that remain in the cold-rolled state to samples that are stress-relieved (annealed sufficiently to relax internal stresses without altering the overall phase) under identical subsequent mechanical tests.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be carried out over a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to ~1273 K, with specific focus at high temperatures ~1250 °C for creep tests) and using comparable strain rates as in earlier studies (e.g., for tensile, compressive, and nano-indentation creep tests).
generation.structural_mediator: The density and spatial organization of residual dislocation networks in the alloy, as modulated by internal thermal stresses resulting from differential thermal expansion.
generation.mechanism: As the alloy cools from high temperatures or undergoes thermal cycling, its intrinsic lattice parameter change (thermal expansion mismatch) produces local internal stresses. These stresses interact with the pre-existing dislocation networks from cold rolling—enhancing dislocation locking and impeding dislocation mobility. At lower temperatures this leads to pronounced work hardening and higher measured hardness, while at elevated temperatures these internal stresses contribute to resisting dislocation glide (thus affecting creep behavior) and modulate the apparent elastic moduli via local strain heterogeneities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens retaining the residual dislocation structure (cold-rolled) will exhibit higher yield strengths, pronounced work hardening, and superior high-temperature creep resistance compared to stress-relieved specimens, which should show lower internal stress levels, reduced dislocation density, and correspondingly lower mechanical strength. Furthermore, measurements of lattice parameter evolution (via in situ diffraction) should reveal internal strain fields correlating with the dislocation density and the measured thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the standard, as-cast/cold-rolled HfNbTaTiZr alloy that has not been modified by post-cold rolling stress-relief annealing or additional thermal cycling.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to govern the behavior of single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloys within the temperature range where no phase transitions occur (~RT to 1273 K). Its relevance may diminish if secondary phase precipitation or significant grain boundary effects (e.g., from coarsening) become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds upon observations of residual dislocation networks and work hardening in cold-rolled HfNbTaTiZr (e.g., evidence in PMC10453588::web::013::3_results and PMC10453588::web::019::4_discussion) and temperature-insensitive elastic moduli from in situ neutron experiments (e.g., PMC11206460::web::000::abstract). The new element proposed here is that the thermal expansion mismatch—previously recognized in composite solidification—actively interacts with these dislocation networks to control both low- and high-temperature mechanical responses. Direct measurements of these internal thermal stresses in HfNbTaTiZr are not yet available, introducing uncertainty in the strength of this coupling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one set remains in the cold-rolled (as-processed) state with high residual dislocation densities, and a second set is stress-relieved via an annealing treatment designed to minimize residual dislocations without altering the BCC phase. Perform identical tensile, creep (at ~1250 °C), microhardness, and in situ diffraction experiments over the full temperature range. Additionally, use high-temperature X-ray or neutron diffraction to directly measure lattice parameter evolution and map internal strain fields.
measurements: Dislocation density (TEM or diffraction line broadening analysis)
Tensile and compression stress–strain curves, including work hardening rates
Creep strain rates at high temperature (~1250 °C)
Elastic moduli via resonant ultrasound or in situ neutron diffraction
Lattice parameter changes with temperature (thermal expansion curves) and associated internal strain mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stress-relieved specimens (with reduced residual dislocation density) display mechanical responses (e.g., yield strength, work hardening rate, creep resistance, and elastic moduli), along with internal strain fields, that are indistinguishable from those of the cold-rolled specimens despite significantly altered dislocation densities, then the proposed coupling between thermal expansion mismatch and residual dislocation structure is not the governing mechanism and the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The differentials between the UTS and YS were about 100 MPa, and gradually widened as the temperature rose. Work hardening appeared in all curves from RT to 1073 K. We speculated that this was due to the fact that the heat treatment did not completely eliminate the residual stress of the alloy after cold rolling [,]. In order to prove this, the rolled samples were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy before a tensile test (see Figure 5). Some obvious dense dislocation bands were found in Figure 5a, and in addition, the diffraction pattern indicated that the alloy retained the structure of a single-phase BCC after the prior treatment. The region where the dislocation band was located was enlarged to further analyze its composition. In Figure 5b, it can be clearly found that the previously thought dislocation band was composed of two rows of dislocations. After a further enlargement, it was found that each dislocation band was composed of dense, short dislocations. This proved the previous conjecture that the residual dislocation after cold rolling caused a work hardening of the alloy.

Figure 9 shows the true stress–strain curves of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA at different deformation strain rates and temperatures. It was found that all curves had similar trends. That is, with the rise of the strain, the flow stress increased to the peak stress first and then decreased as the strain continued to increase. Before it reached the peak stress, the flow stress rose along with the strain. At this stage, the dislocation density increased due to deformation, the dislocation accumulation increased the deformation resistance, and a work hardening was the main rheological feature. When the flow stress achieved its maximal stress, it steadily declined as the strain increased. This is attributed to the dynamic recovery or dynamic recrystallization softening mechanism in the material exceeding the work-hardening mechanism, which is macrographically manifested as a gradual reduction in the flow stress []. In fact, the process of thermal deformation of materials is a competitive process of work-hardening and softening mechanisms, and the effects of hardening and softening reach an equilibrium when the flow stress reaches the peak stress []. The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results.
